name: Omar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on the contact-centre calls and chats. I finished secondary school and moved into this work after years at an appliance-parts counter. I am good at listening to a customer describe a broken machine, but still slow when a refund crosses two payment screens. My Friday-night cover rate makes the pay higher than usual, and I use an AI draft occasionally after a colleague shows me which dates to verify.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is at stake after you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Grete runs a small lunch stall, and our grown children live in their own flats. We rent and have nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of call centres are within a bus ride. I would like fewer Friday nights one day, but we have no settled income for leaving full-time work; I like a call that ends with a replacement part in the right customer’s hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Friday desk AI Plateau sounds like the draft we sometimes use for a part-number reply. I would still check the actual order before promising a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid Friday nights remain. Nine months saved means one poor week at Grete’s stall will not force us to ask the children for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking replacement calls and reading the order beside occasional AI drafts. In the first year of small change, I’d ask a senior agent to check one two-screen refund with me during a paid Friday shift each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable about our income, still learning the tricky screen. The wrong part number can make a neat answer useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part number did the draft miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the draft used the old model number from the first call. I found the newer number only because a senior agent made me open the latest order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grete (my wife) and I keep the nine-month reserve for an actual gap in wages. We will not spend it just because the reply takes less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will answer the straightforward parts calls first. I would ask the supervisor to show how many paid Friday hours remain before calling the change efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the Friday premium could shrink even if I still work here. Nine months saved gives Grete and me time to compare nearby centres, but her stall income changes week to week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d test the new parts matcher on fifteen old wrong-item orders during a paid shift if the supervisor lets me log mistakes. In the first year routine calls move, I’d keep my current Friday shifts while comparing the written weekly wage and hours of posted jobs at three nearby centres; I would apply only if Friday hours fall and another posting covers rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the premium, curious about a proper test. An unchanged badge can still come with a shorter paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the matcher test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count how often the matcher chose the wrong model and how many customers called again. A fast part number is no help if it belongs to another machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare postings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full weekly pay after bus fare, not just the hourly rate. The extra Friday money is part of our rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Friday team AGI by 2028 could choose the right appliance part and explain it before I answer. I would ask for written shift dates and actual posted wages at nearby shops and centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior calls could vanish in 2028. Robots around 2031 may later reach hands-on stock work, but nine months saved gives us some room to choose where I work next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d put the last eight weekly wage slips beside three posted paid parts-counter jobs to see whether their hours cover rent and bills. In the first year after 2028, if paid Friday calls end, I’d use at most four weeks of our existing savings for a focused search and apply to a posted parts-counter job only if its written weekly wage and hours still cover rent and bus fare; I would leave current paid calls only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about losing the premium, not desperate to grab the first job. Four weeks of savings can buy a careful search, not a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect at a counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would visit each counter to see whether staff also lift stock or only answer screens. If the posting hides heavy work, I need to know before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sets the search limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grete (my wife) and I would agree on the four-week search limit together. Our grown children have their own rent, so the budget rests on our savings and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to learn which nearby shop truly pays for a person to fit the right part. I would ask employers to let me see a whole paid counter rota before I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could become faster at refund screens over five years, but full AGI could handle them in 2031 anyway. Robots around 2034 come later for carrying parts, and I cannot assume that buys me a permanent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep working Friday calls and ask a senior agent to coach one disputed order each paid week. In the first year after 2031, if my paid hours shrink, I’d apply for a posted paid parts-counter role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent after bus fare; I’d stay on current calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful rather than frightened, with time to learn my current work. Five years lets me improve at refunds without paying for a course nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would weekly coaching cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would trace a refund through the payment screen and the replacement order with the senior agent. That is more useful to me than a certificate for an unnamed job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grete compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the actual posted week with Grete (my wife). A short job nearby can still pay less than my Friday shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time to leave the Friday-night rota without a rushed move. I would compare weekday shifts at the nearby centres each year while the premium still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could work fewer nights before I stop full-time work, but I do not know what would replace the wage if I stopped altogether. Nine months saved lets us accept a smaller premium later only if our actual bills still fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the Friday calls and work out the lowest whole weekly wage that covers rent, food and bus fare with Grete. In the first year after 2036, if calls shrink, I’d apply for a posted paid weekday call role only if written weekly wage and hours cover those costs, leaving Friday calls only after a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady about the next few years, watchful about the later rota. A decade before AGI reaches my calls gives me time to choose fewer nights, not a pension I can name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare about weekdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole weekday pay packet with the Friday one, not just count days off. Grete (my wife) would bring her stall figures to the same table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family cover a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have separate bills. We would not put their wages into a calculation for my future work hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it can both answer the parts question and check the refund I am still learning. Nine months saved lets us search without taking the first offer, but the flat still needs rent. Written paid-hour notice and real posted weekly wages at nearby employers would help me compare before a cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the wrong part number after a machine says the order is complete. A customer cannot fit a tidy case note into a broken washing machine.

headlineQuote: A customer cannot fit a tidy case note into a broken washing machine.
portrait: At **58**, Omar is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and appliance-parts work.
He and Grete rent with **nine months saved** and a higher Friday-night rate.
He uses **AI occasionally** but still needs help across two refund screens.
He can **compare nearby jobs** before changing to a weaker wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take parts calls and the refund checks he is still learning.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour notice** and posted roles with real weekly wages would help.
